clue.text: Light shed by Swinnerton

definitions.meaning: a light is a window, here a hinged window frame
a work given out by Frank Swinnerton: his 1911 novel bears this title

explanation.walkthrough: Frank Swinnerton was an English novelist and critic; 'shed by' plays on light being shed, while meaning a book he produced.
explanation.definitionFit: A light is the glazed opening of a window, and a hinged window frame is one such light.

clue.text: Revealed by Alex Kava

definitions.meaning: a thriller of that title written by the American novelist Alex Kava

explanation.definitionFit: Something revealed has been laid bare, uncovered for all to see; it is also the title of a Kava crime novel.

clue.text: Hear Verne dismantling Belgian poet

indicators.note: taking apart the two words and rebuilding them signals that their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone listening to Jules Verne picks his work to pieces in front of a poet from Belgium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dismantling' rearranges the nine letters of HEAR and VERNE.
explanation.definitionFit: Emile Verhaeren was a Symbolist writer from Belgium, famed for his verse.

clue.text: Baker holding notes for tourist

indicators.note: the name Baker holds the notes inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: taken as written
E, D and E are musical notes of the scale

explanation.surface: A baker keeps some notes on hand for a visitor from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Baker' looks like a person but is simply the outer word; 'holding' signals the notes go inside it. 'for tourist' defines by purpose: the guide is for travellers.
explanation.definitionFit: Karl Baedeker's guidebooks were so standard for travellers that the name became a byword for a travel guide.

clue.text: Fitzgerald hero takes the plunge?

definitions.meaning: Dick, the psychiatrist hero of Tender is the Night by F. Scott Fitzgerald, bears this surname
one who plunges into water, the question mark flagging a noun read off a verb phrase

explanation.definitionFit: A swimmer who plunges headfirst into water is one; Dick of that name is the hero of Tender is the Night.

clue.text: Have our cake and recook it for beat writer

indicators.note: cooking the cake again turns its letters over into a fresh mixture

explanation.surface: A bohemian author wants to have his cake and eat it, then bakes it all again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recook it' rearranges OURCAKE; 'Have' and 'and' are link words in the proverb-shaped surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack Kerouac wrote On the Road and was a central figure of the Beat Generation of American writers.

clue.text: We only what is inevitable " (Henry Miller)

definitions.text: We only what is inevitable " (Henry Miller)

parts.words: We only what is inevitable " (Henry Miller)
parts.note: a quotation from the American novelist with one verb missing after 'only', which the solver supplies

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank clue: the gap after 'We only' takes a verb meaning to fight against or withstand.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb means to fight against or withstand, completing the line from the American novelist.

clue.text: Steadfast wife animated as novelist

parts.note: Penelope, the wife of Odysseus, stayed faithful through his twenty-year absence
animated means full of life, spirited

explanation.surface: A faithful wife is described as full of life, like a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' is a link word. Penelope Lively is a Booker-winning English writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Penelope Lively is an English author of fiction, Booker winner for Moon Tiger.

clue.text: Comic strip character valued above Claudio's friend

parts.note: super is Latin for above and also means excellent, highly valued
Hero is Claudio's beloved in Shakespeare's Much Ado About Nothing

explanation.surface: A cartoon figure is prized more highly than a Shakespearean lover's sweetheart.
explanation.definitionFit: A caped crusader with special powers is the stock figure of strip cartoons.

clue.text: He suffered at the hands of Hermann the German in Balaclava (Russia) ()

definitions.text: He suffered at the hands of Hermann the German

indicators.note: the name sits inside the run of letters of these two words, read straight across

explanation.surface: A victim of a German warlord turns up wearing a woolly hat in Russia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points into balaclaVA RUSsia. Hermann is the German name for Arminius, who destroyed three Roman legions in the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9.
explanation.definitionFit: Publius Quinctilius Varus was the Roman general whose legions Arminius wiped out, after which he killed himself.

clue.text: Percy put his in the bottle

definitions.text: Percy put his in the bottle

parts.words: Percy put his in the bottle
parts.note: Percy Bysshe Shelley launched his political pamphlets sealed in bottles on the sea, a written note sent adrift

explanation.walkthrough: Percy is Percy Bysshe Shelley, who in 1812 set his radical Declaration of Rights afloat in bottles off the Devon coast.
explanation.definitionFit: A written communication sent adrift sealed in glass is the classic note in a bottle.

clue.text: Arts return to American ship due to German composer

indicators.note: the word Arts comes back on itself, read from end to start

parts.note: taken as written
USS stands for United States Ship, the prefix of American naval vessels

explanation.surface: Culture comes back to an American vessel because of a German musician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns ARTS into STRA. 'to' and 'due to' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Strauss was the German who wrote Der Rosenkavalier and Also sprach Zarathustra.

clue.text: He fights the good fight

parts.note: a campaigner for causes: here the American consumer advocate Ralph, scourge of unsafe cars

explanation.walkthrough: Ralph Nader is the American consumer-rights campaigner whose book Unsafe at Any Speed took on the car industry.
explanation.definitionFit: Ralph Nader has spent his career crusading for consumers' rights against big business.

clue.text: Colin Platt analysed its marks, citing Adam Smith

definitions.text: Colin Platt analysed its marks, citing Adam Smith

parts.words: Colin Platt analysed its marks, citing Adam Smith
parts.note: the historian Colin Platt's book on late-medieval heraldry and display is titled Marks of this quality, a word Smith uses for wealth

explanation.walkthrough: Adam Smith uses the word for national wealth in The Wealth of Nations; Colin Platt's study of medieval display is Marks of Opulence.
explanation.definitionFit: Great wealth and lavish display are what the word means, Smith's term for a nation's riches.

clue.text: Comic book looked on, sharply observing

parts.note: The Eagle was a celebrated British boys' comic of the 1950s, home of Dan Dare
eyed means looked at, watched

explanation.surface: Someone peers keenly over a reader's shoulder at a comic.
explanation.walkthrough: The Eagle was a famous British boys' comic, launched in 1950.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with a raptor's keen sight misses nothing, so is sharp-sighted and watchful.

clue.text: Rivers diverted by her

parts.note: St John Rivers, the clergyman in Charlotte Bronte's novel, is turned aside by the heroine who refuses to marry him

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rivers' looks like waterways to be diverted, but it is St John Rivers, whose proposal and missionary plans the heroine turns down.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlotte Bronte's heroine refuses her cousin St John Rivers, deflecting his plans for her.

clue.text: Grain source for Patricia and Bernard

parts.note: corn is cereal grain
a well is a source, as of water or information

explanation.surface: Two writers are named as the source of grain.
explanation.walkthrough: Patricia Cornwell writes crime fiction and Bernard Cornwell historical novels; 'for' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Patricia, the crime novelist, and Bernard, the historical novelist, share this surname.

clue.text: Not the way to present Beckett's Hamm

definitions.text: Not the way to present Beckett's Hamm

parts.words: Not the way to present Beckett's Hamm
parts.note: Hamm, in Endgame, sounds like a ham actor, but playing him with exaggeration would be wrong

explanation.walkthrough: Hamm is the central character of Samuel Beckett's Endgame; his name suggests a 'ham', an actor who exaggerates.
explanation.definitionFit: To ham it up is to exaggerate a stage role, which is what the name Hamm tempts an actor to do.

clue.text: Streatfeild's child star who took a bow

definitions.text: Streatfeild's child star who took a bow

parts.words: Streatfeild's child star who took a bow
parts.note: the title heroine of Noel Streatfeild's novel, a former child film actress

explanation.walkthrough: Noel Streatfeild, author of Ballet Shoes, wrote a 1968 novel named after its child-star heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of Noel Streatfeild's 1968 children's book is a former child film star.

clue.text: Strange Zion man whose fame rests on one book

definitions.text: whose fame rests on one book

indicators.note: something strange is odd or out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An odd figure from Zion is remembered for a single volume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' rearranges ZIONMAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Alessandro Manzoni is known chiefly for one novel, I Promessi Sposi (The Betrothed).

clue.text: On demand in heroic story like a lyric poem

indicators.note: the abbreviation goes inside the story's word

parts.note: an epic is a long heroic narrative
OD is a common abbreviation for on demand

explanation.surface: Something requested on the spot turns up within a grand saga that resembles a short poem.
explanation.walkthrough: An epode is a lyric poem in which a long line alternates with a shorter one; 'in' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: An epode is a lyric form, and the adjective describes verse in that alternating-line style.

clue.text: Badly riled up in introductions

indicators.note: the letters are put together badly, in the wrong order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is upset over the opening speeches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly' rearranges RILEDUP.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian plural of the word for a musical opening piece, as in the titles of Debussy's piano works.

clue.text: Early dramatist in proud allegory

indicators.note: the name lies inside the letters of these two words

explanation.surface: An old playwright is found in a lofty symbolic tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points into prOUD ALLegory.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicholas Udall wrote Ralph Roister Doister, one of the first English stage comedies, in the sixteenth century.

clue.text: Belief in restraint for White's raptor

definitions.meaning: an archaic word for faith or credence, from the French
a long cord tethering a hawk in training, as in T. H. White's The Goshawk

explanation.walkthrough: T. H. White's The Goshawk describes his attempts to train a hawk on a long training line; 'in' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word once meant faith or trust, and in falconry it names the long training line on a hawk.

clue.text: I dip into maritime lawyer to identify huntress

indicators.note: the letter plunges into the lawyer's name, going inside it

parts.note: Richard Henry Dana Jr, author of Two Years Before the Mast, practised as a maritime lawyer

explanation.surface: I take a plunge into the world of a sea lawyer to spot a woman who hunts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dip into' puts I inside DANA; 'to identify' is a link phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman goddess of the chase, counterpart of the Greek Artemis.

clue.text: They sang for Sassoon

parts.note: Siegfried Sassoon's poem opens with the line that all of them, without exception, suddenly burst out singing

explanation.walkthrough: Siegfried Sassoon's 1919 poem Everyone Sang begins 'Everyone suddenly burst out singing'.
explanation.definitionFit: All people without exception, the subject of Sassoon's poem in which all burst out singing.

clue.text: Bloomer in Swann's language of love

definitions.text: Bloomer in Swann's language of love

parts.words: Bloomer in Swann's language of love
parts.note: an orchid that Swann and Odette, in Proust, turn into their private phrase for making love

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' looks like a blunder, but it is a flower: in Proust, Swann and Odette say 'do a ...' for making love.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a showy orchid, a flowering plant whose name becomes Swann's code for lovemaking.

clue.text: Laertes not the man to touch, if he respected it

definitions.text: Laertes not the man to touch, if he respected it

parts.words: Laertes not the man to touch, if he respected it
parts.note: Polonius tells his son Laertes 'Neither a borrower nor a lender be', so a son heeding him would lend nothing to one who touched him for money

explanation.walkthrough: To touch someone is to ask them for a loan; Polonius's counsel to Laertes in Hamlet forbids lending.
explanation.definitionFit: Counsel or guidance, here the famous precepts Polonius gives his departing son in Hamlet.
